name: Kristiansund
title: Thickness Gauging Kristiansund | Norwegian Sea Supply Vessels
description: Thickness gauging in Kristiansund for supply vessels, standby ships, fishing vessels and coastal ships: tank, deck and hull UTM at Vestbase and town quays.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Offshore and Coastal Vessels in Kristiansund
intro: Kristiansund, built on several islands facing the Norwegian Sea, is the supply port for the oil and gas fields of the Norwegian Sea and a fishing town long known for klippfisk. Supply, standby and subsea vessels work from Vestbase, while fishing vessels, coastal cargo ships and the coastal express use the town's sheltered harbour. Atlantis sends its technicians from India to Kristiansund for each job, and they meet the vessel at whichever base or quay it lies.

highlights.h: Vestbase and the Norwegian Sea fields
highlights.p: Vestbase at Vikan, on Nordlandet, has supported Norwegian Sea installations since 1980, from Draugen and Heidrun to Åsgard, Njord and Kristin. Supply vessels lying at its quays between runs are the most common gauging job in Kristiansund.

Standby and emergency response vessels spend long periods on station near the fields and come in for crew changes and maintenance. Their ballast and fuel tanks and the deck structure around rescue zones see constant wear, and a port stay is the time to measure them.

highlights.h: Klippfisk town with a working fleet
highlights.p: Fishing vessels and fish carriers have used Kristiansund's harbour for centuries, and the fleet still lands catches and maintains vessels here. Holds, refrigerated tanks and seawater piping can be gauged alongside during a lay period, often in preparation for a docking further south.

port.h: Kristiansund: island harbour and Norwegian Sea supply port
p: Kristiansund lies on the outer coast of Nordmøre, where a cluster of islands encloses a sheltered harbour reached from the Norwegian Sea through narrow sounds. The town has lived from the sea for centuries; its merchants built their wealth on klippfisk, cod salted and dried on the shore rocks and shipped to southern Europe and beyond. The oil and gas industry added a second economy. Vestbase, at Vikan on Nordlandet, was chosen as the supply base for Draugen and Heidrun and opened in 1980, and the town has been the logistics centre for Norwegian Sea operations ever since, with offshore crew flights operating from the airport close by.

Offshore vessels make up much of the working traffic: platform supply vessels running cargo to the fields, anchor handlers and subsea vessels for drilling and installation campaigns, and standby vessels rotating on and off station. A second supply base on neighbouring Averøy serves operators and service companies as well. Fishing vessels and fish carriers use the harbour, coastal cargo ships and tankers bring fuel and goods to the region, and the coastal express calls on its way between Bergen and Kirkenes. Along the coast towards Trondheim, the methanol plant at Tjeldbergodden ships its product by tanker, and the Nyhamna gas plant near Molde lies within reach to the south-west.

Vessels stay in Kristiansund for days rather than hours when they are between runs, waiting on weather or changing crews, and for longer when a charter ends. Winter in the Norwegian Sea is hard on vessels and on schedules: storms close the offshore cargo windows, supply vessels wait in port, and that waiting time is useful for tank work. The harbour stays free of ice, and midwinter daylight is short, so work on exposed decks is planned for the light hours while tanks and machinery spaces carry on under lighting. In summer, drilling and installation campaigns bring more vessels but less spare time aboard each, so gauging fits more easily into the quieter months.

facilities.h: Where vessels are gauged in Kristiansund
p: Vestbase offers the quay space, cranes and storage that offshore logistics need, and for gauging that means safe access to a vessel lying still with its crew aboard. Between runs, crews can usually free up ballast tanks, chain lockers and empty cargo tanks for entry; longer stays allow bulk and liquid tanks to be cleaned and opened in sequence. The supply base on Averøy offers a similar setting for the vessels working from it, and the town quays suit fishing vessels and coastal ships.

Kristiansund's gauging work is mostly done afloat. For dry-docking, owners of supply vessels and fishing vessels from this coast often use the yards of the Møre region around Ålesund and Ulsteinvik, or yards further afield, and readings taken in Kristiansund can serve as the pre-docking steel estimate that the yard and class surveyor work from. When the offshore market is weak, idle vessels are sometimes moored in sheltered waters near the town, and bringing one back into service is a full-scope job that begins with gauging.
list: Vestbase quays at Vikan — tank, chain locker and deck gauging on platform supply and subsea vessels between runs or charters.
Kristiansund Base on Averøy — gauging on supply and project vessels working from the base.
Town and fishing quays — fish hold, tank and piping readings on fishing vessels and fish carriers alongside.
Commercial quays — deck, hold and ballast tank measurement on coastal cargo ships and tankers during discharge.
Sheltered moorings near the town — reactivation gauging on laid-up offshore vessels, reached by boat.

context.h: Norwegian Sea operations and the rules around them
p: Kristiansund is north of 62°N, beyond the North Sea emission control area. Port state control on foreign ships calling here is carried out by the Norwegian Maritime Authority as part of the Paris MoU, but most vessels working from the bases are Norwegian-flagged, and for them the Authority acts as flag state. The offshore installations they serve answer to Havtil, the Norwegian Ocean Industry Authority, while the vessels themselves are regulated as ships; the operators bring the two together in their contracts, which spell out the vessel standards, audits and documentation they expect from shipowners.

The Norwegian Sea is harsher than the North Sea in winter, and vessels working there take a beating: slamming loads on the bow, green water on deck and constant motion straining cargo rails, tank structure and deck equipment foundations. Supply vessels on long charters may spend years on this run between dockings. When an owner is renewing a charter or bidding for a new one, documented thickness readings and crack detection at highly loaded details give the charterer evidence of condition, and give the owner a basis for planning steel renewal at the next docking.

jobs.p: Most Kristiansund jobs are on offshore vessels and are organised around the gaps in their schedules: a few days between runs in winter, the end of a charter, or the weeks before a docking. Fishing vessels and coastal cargo ships make up the rest. The owner or manager defines the scope with us beforehand, the crew prepare the spaces, and the team works through them in priority order so that the most important readings are secured even if the vessel is called back offshore early. Results go to the superintendent each day while the work continues. Examples:
list: A platform supply vessel waiting on weather at Vestbase: ballast tanks and chain lockers gauged during the delay, with the rest of the scope planned for the next port stay.
An anchor handler at the end of a drilling campaign: stern roller structure, work deck plating and towing pin foundations measured, with MPI at highly loaded welds.
A standby vessel in for crew change and maintenance: fuel and ballast tanks gauged, and deck plating around the rescue zone measured.
A fish carrier alongside the town quays: hold and tank structure readings to prepare a steel estimate for a docking at a Møre yard.
A laid-up subsea vessel near the town: reactivation survey gauging of tanks, decks and seawater systems before a return to charter.

logistics: Kristiansund Airport, Kvernberget, lies on Nordlandet near Vestbase and has domestic flights to Oslo and Bergen, so the team reaches the base soon after landing. Vestbase and the Averøy base apply ISPS and site access rules, and the agent or the base registers the team in advance. Norway is in the Schengen area, and technicians travelling from India need Schengen visas; offshore owners who expect winter port stays benefit from having visas in place before a specific vessel needs them.

faqs.q: Can a supply vessel be gauged at Vestbase during a weather delay?
faqs.a: Yes, and winter weather delays are often the best opportunity. When offshore cargo work stops, a vessel may lie alongside for a day or more, and the crew can open ballast tanks and chain lockers. Because the vessel could be called out as soon as the weather improves, the scope is ordered by priority and agreed with the master, so whatever has been measured is complete and reportable.

faqs.q: Where do Kristiansund vessels go for dry-docking?
faqs.a: Owners choose their yard, and for this part of the coast that is often one of the yards around Ålesund and Ulsteinvik, or a yard further afield. We travel to the docking yard when the owner wants the full programme done there, and readings taken in Kristiansund beforehand let the yard and class plan steel renewal before the vessel arrives.

faqs.q: Which details on Norwegian Sea vessels are worth measuring?
faqs.a: On supply and anchor-handling vessels, the bow area, cargo rails, work deck plating and the foundations of deck machinery take the brunt of the weather, while ballast tanks and chain lockers corrode steadily. Combining thickness readings with magnetic particle testing at highly loaded welds gives a clearer picture than either method alone, especially on vessels that have worked through several winters without docking.

faqs.q: Do you gauge fishing vessels in Kristiansund?
faqs.a: Yes. Fishing vessels and fish carriers alongside the town quays can have holds, refrigerated tanks, double bottom tanks and seawater piping measured while they are idle. The readings are tied to the vessel's drawings and can be passed to the yard chosen for the next docking, so the owner knows the extent of any steel renewal before committing to a dock date.
